patient_summary:
Hello there, you had a little check-up today to help find out what was causing your tummy pain and bleeding. A doctor used a special tool called an endoscope to look inside your throat, stomach, and colon. They also took some tiny pieces of tissue to check if there was anything unusual.

You didn't need any special medicines for this check-up. The doctor used a special tool to look inside your body, and they didn't find anything wrong with your esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. But they did find a small, round growth in your rectum, which they removed using a special tool. They also took some tissue samples to check if you had any infections.

You didn't need any blood transfusions or surgery, and you felt okay after the procedure. The doctor will talk to your parents next week about the results and what to do next. If you have any more pain or bleeding, or if you have any other concerns, you should tell your parents or the doctor right away. Also, the doctor estimated that you lost about 5 mL of blood during the procedure.
caregiver_checklist: Give the patient a liquid diet for 2 days after the procedure.
Check for signs of abdominal pain or bleeding within 24 hours.
Watch for signs of infection such as fever or redness at the site.
Call if the patient develops severe abdominal pain or bleeding.
Schedule a follow-up appointment to discuss biopsy results and further management.
Call if the patient has any unusual symptoms or signs of complications.
Watch for signs of dehydration, such as dry mouth or decreased urination.
Call if the patient shows signs of dehydration or other complications.
Schedule a colonoscopy follow-up in 6 months.
child_explanation: You had a tummy ache and some blood in your poop. The doctors are checking your inside to find out why. They used a long, thin tube to look at your tummy and colon. It's like when you look through a telescope. They took tiny pieces to check under a microscope. Everything looks normal now, except for a small bump. They fixed that too. The doctors and grown-ups are taking good care of you. You'll hear more about it next week.
source_text: PROCEDURES:,  Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsy and polypectomy.,REASON FOR PROCEDURE: , Child with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding.  Rule out inflammatory bowel disease, allergic enterocolitis, rectal polyps, and rectal vascular malformations.,CONSENT:,  History and physical examination was performed.  The procedure, indications, alternatives available, and complications, i.e. bleeding, perforation, infection, adverse medication reaction, the possible need for blood transfusion, and surgery should a complication occur were discussed with the parents who understood and indicated this.  Opportunity for questions was provided and informed consent was obtained.,MEDICATION:  ,General anesthesia.,INSTRUMENT: , Olympus GIF-160.,COMPLICATIONS:,  None.,FINDINGS: , With the patient in the supine position and intubated, the endoscope was inserted without difficulty into the hypopharynx.  The esophageal mucosa and vascular pattern appeared normal.  The lower esophageal sphincter was located at 25 cm from the central incisors.  It appeared normal.  A Z-line was identified within the lower esophageal sphincter.  The endoscope was advanced into the stomach, which distended with excess air.  Rugal folds flattened completely.  Gastric mucosa appeared normal throughout.  No hiatal hernia was noted.  Pyloric valve appeared normal.  The endoscope was advanced into the first, second, and third portions of duodenum, which had normal mucosa, coloration, and fold pattern.  Biopsies were obtained x2 in the second portion of duodenum, antrum, and distal esophagus at 22 cm from the central incisors for histology.  Additional 2 biopsies were obtained for CLO testing in the antrum.  Excess air was evacuated from the stomach.  The scope was removed from the patient who tolerated that part of procedure well.  The patient was turned and the scope was advanced with some difficulty to the terminal ileum.  The terminal ileum mucosa and the colonic mucosa throughout was normal except at approximately 10 cm where a 1 x 1 cm pedunculated juvenile-appearing polyp was noted.  Biopsies were obtained x2 in the terminal ileum, cecum, ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid, and rectum.  Then, the polyp was snared right at the base of the polyp on the stalk and 20 watts of pure coag was applied in 2-second bursts x3.  The polyp was severed.  There was no bleeding at the stalk after removal of the polyp head.  The polyp head was removed by suction.  Excess air was evacuated from the colon.  The patient tolerated that part of the procedure well and was taken to recovery in satisfactory condition.  Estimated blood loss approximately 5 mL.,IMPRESSION: , Normal esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as terminal ileum except for a 1 x 1-cm rectal polyp, which was removed successfully by polypectomy snare.,PLAN:  ,Histologic evaluation and CLO testing.  I will contact the parents next week with biopsy results and further management plans will be discussed at that time.
